healthcare.summary: Complete health & medication guide for traveling to Tanzania. Emergency numbers (112/111/999), yellow fever requirements, pharmacy tips, restricted medications, malaria precautions, and travel insurance advice.

connectivity.simOptions: Vodacom or Airtel prepaid SIMs at Julius Nyerere Airport or any phone shop. Need passport. Very cheap data plans.
connectivity.wifiAvailability: Free WiFi at most hotels and lodges. Limited in safari camps and national parks. Zanzibar towns have decent connectivity.
connectivity.bestOption: Vodacom prepaid SIM for best coverage including safari areas. Buy at airport. Don't rely on WiFi during safari.

cultural.tipping: 10% at restaurants. Safari guides: $15-25/day per person. Kilimanjaro porters: $8-15/day. Hotel porters: TZS 2000-5000.
cultural.dressCode: Modest dress, especially on Zanzibar (Muslim culture) — cover shoulders and knees. Safari: neutral colors (khaki, olive, brown). Avoid blue/black (attracts tsetse flies).
cultural.greetings: 'Jambo' (hello) or 'Habari' (how are you) — response is 'Nzuri' (fine). Handshake is common. Elders are addressed with respect.
taboos: Photographing people without permission (especially Maasai — tip expected)
cultural.haggling: Expected at markets, souvenir shops, and with taxi/tuk-tuk drivers. Not at restaurants or supermarkets. Start at 30-50% of asking price.

practical.visaFreeCountries: US citizens: visa on arrival ($50) or e-Visa. UK, EU, most nationalities eligible for visa on arrival.
practical.bestTimeToVisit: June-October (dry season, best for safari and Kilimanjaro). January-February (short dry season, calving in Serengeti). Avoid March-May (heavy rains).

hospitals.name: Aga Khan Hospital Dar es Salaam
hospitals.notes: Best hospital for tourists in Tanzania. English-speaking staff, international standard care.

hospitals.name: Muhimbili National Hospital
hospitals.address: United Nations Road, Upanga West, Dar es Salaam
hospitals.notes: Tanzania's national referral hospital. Use for emergencies only — limited English.

immediate: Move to higher ground during heavy rain
Do not cross flooded roads or streams
Follow Tanzania Red Cross and local authority guidance
after: Boil or purify drinking water after flooding
Avoid contact with floodwater — cholera and leptospirosis risk
Seek medical attention promptly if showing signs of waterborne illness

steps: File a police report immediately — get the report number, you will need it
Contact the US Embassy or nearest consulate: Contact the nearest US Embassy
Bring the police report + any ID you have (driver's license, copy of passport)
Apply for an Emergency Passport (usually issued within 1-2 business days)
Notify your travel insurance and airline of the situation
stolenPassport.notes: Keep a digital copy of your passport in cloud storage (Google Photos, iCloud) and email yourself a scan before travel.

steps: Go to the nearest police station (or call 112)
Bring ID or a copy of your passport if available
Request a written report — ask for an English copy or certified translation if needed
Keep the report number safe — required for insurance claims
For theft: list all stolen items with approximate values
policeReport.notes: In many countries, tourist police stations are available in major cities — they have English-speaking staff. Ask your hotel concierge for the nearest tourist police.

steps: If involved in an accident: do not move vehicles if anyone is injured
Call police (112) and ambulance (114) if there are injuries
Exchange contact, license, and insurance details with other parties
Document the scene with photos before moving vehicles
Contact your rental car company's emergency line
Contact your travel insurance's 24h assistance line
roadsideAssistance.notes: Traffic drives on the LEFT. An International Driving Permit (IDP) is required for most foreign licenses. Rental vehicles are available at major airports and cities.
